title: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: Was It Really Zhuge Liang?
description:
Romance of the Three Kingdoms, chapter 46: thick fog, twenty boats lined with bundles of straw, a fleet that turns around to take arrows on its other side, and "Thank you, Chancellor, for the arrows." This episode follows that one turn backwards through the records. The standard edition says five or six thousand arrows per boat and more than 100,000 carried ashore; in the Jiajing edition, with its preface of 1522, Kongming says "over 100,000", but the count on shore is "more than 90,000". In the Yuan-dynasty storytellers' Sanguozhi Pinghua (c. 1321–1323), the one who turns his boat to take arrows before the Battle of Red Cliffs and shouts "Chancellor, thanks for the arrows" is Zhou Yu. Go back further, to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Sun Quan, the entry for Ruxu in Jian'an 18 (213): Pei Songzhi's note quotes the Weilüe. Sun Quan sails a large boat to look at Cao Cao's camp, the boat takes so many arrows it nearly capsizes, he turns it to take arrows on the other side, and "once the arrows were even and the boat level, he went back". No fog, no straw, no numbers, no thanks. Yet the Wu Li, quoted in the same note, says Cao Cao ordered that "no bow or crossbow may shoot at will", and that Sun Quan came in a light boat. Pei Songzhi copied both accounts; when Sima Guang wrote about Ruxu in the Zizhi Tongjian, he left both out and gave no reason. That year Zhuge Liang and Guan Yu were guarding Jing Province, and Zhou Yu had died in 210. The earliest boat to turn and take arrows belongs to Sun Quan at Ruxu, and only one book, the Weilüe, says so. File closed.

The official histories and the Zizhi Tongjian follow the Daizhige transcriptions (of the Siku Quanshu editions); the Pinghua follows a Daizhige transcription; the Jiajing edition follows a Wikisource transcription (not checked against scans); the standard edition follows Project Gutenberg. Earlier plays such as Yuan drama were not checked. Sources are listed below; sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

Information as of 2026-10-20

cj101.text: In Romance of the Three Kingdoms, before dawn, day 3, fog fills the Yangtze.

cj102.text: Twenty fast boats near Cao's camp, straw-lined, under blue cloth.

cj103.text: Cao's camp can't see, so his archers shoot blindly.

cj104.text: Arrows fall like rain; then the fleet turns to take arrows on its other side.

cj105.text: Fog lifting, the men shout: Thanks for the arrows, Chancellor!

cj107.text: In the earliest Ming edition, how many arrows were counted on shore?

cj108.text: In a storyteller's book 700 years ago, who's at the bow?

cj109.text: 1,000+ years earlier, a book tells of a big boat nearly tipped by arrows.

cj110.text: On the same page, another book says Cao Cao gave an order.

cj111.text: That year, where was Zhuge Liang?

cj112.text: Straw boats and arrows: not Zhuge Liang?

cj201.text: In today's standard novel, it's him: chapter 46 is "Kongming Borrows Arrows with a Clever Plan."

cj202.text: Zhou Yu wants a pretext to kill him,

cj203.text: so asks for 100,000 arrows within ten days.

cj204.text: Zhuge Liang says three days is enough, and signs a pledge to be punished if he fails.

cj205.text: Zhou Yu even tells the craftsmen to stall and hold back materials.

cj206.text: Those twenty straw boats he borrowed from Lu Su, with just 30 men each.

cj208.text: The novel says he'd foreseen three days ago that fog would come.

cj209.text: That arrow rain? Fearing an ambush in the fog, Cao Cao brought 10,000+ archers from his land camps.

cj210.text: After three days, how many did he deliver?

cj211.text: The standard edition: about 5,000–6,000 per boat; over 100,000 carried ashore.

cj212.text: Zhou Yu can only sigh: I'm no match.

cj213.text: But that earliest Ming edition we mentioned gives different numbers.

cj214.text: It's the Jiajing-era edition, with a preface dated 1522.

cj215.text: Kongming says: 4,000–5,000 a boat, over 100,000 in all;

cj216.text: but what's carried ashore to the command tent is just over 90,000.

cj217.text: Two numbers in one passage, and they don't match.

cj218.text: Oddly, here the section is titled "Zhuge Liang Outwits Zhou Yu,"

cj220.text: But did anyone write that turn before this novel?

cj301.text: Yes. 700 years ago, the Yuan storytellers' book Sanguozhi Pinghua wrote it.

cj302.text: We asked who stood at the bow: it's Zhou Yu.

cj303.text: Before Red Cliffs, after trading shouts, Zhou Yu sails out: one big boat, ten small.

cj304.text: On Cao's side, thousands are told to shoot at once.

cj305.text: Left side full, he turns; the right takes arrows.

cj306.text: Before long the boats bristle with arrows; the Pinghua says several million.

cj307.text: Zhou Yu calls out: Chancellor, thanks for the arrows!

cj308.text: Cao Cao, furious, orders: fight tomorrow and get them back.

cj309.text: No fog here, no straw, just curtains on the boats; and no three-day deadline.

cj310.text: It's a battle; Zhou Yu isn't out to trick anyone out of arrows.

cj312.text: In the Pinghua he's on early, even urging Zhou Yu to war;

cj313.text: he just has no part in the arrows scene.

cj314.text: In versions we found, only the Ming novel gives the scene to Zhuge Liang.

cj315.text: But before the Pinghua, did anyone write of a boat turning to take arrows?

cj401.text: Yes, in a note to a history book: the first month of Jian'an 18, the year 213, at Ruxu.

cj402.text: The year before, on Lü Meng's advice, Sun Quan built a fort at the Ruxu river mouth.

cj404.text: By then, Red Cliffs was five years in the past.

cj406.text: Chen Shou just says Cao Cao saw Sun Quan's orderly army, sighed, and withdrew.

cj407.text: Cao's chapter: he took Sun Quan's camp west of the river, caught a commander, withdrew.

cj408.text: No arrows on either side, no boat. So where are the arrows?

cj409.text: In the notes Pei Songzhi added two centuries later;

cj410.text: he copied in from other books what Chen Shou left out.

cj411.text: Under this, he quotes the Weilüe, by Yu Huan, a man of Wei; the book is now lost.

cj412.text: Sun Quan comes in a big boat to view Cao's camp; Cao's archers shoot; arrows stick fast.

cj413.text: One side gets so heavy it nearly tips; that's the big boat we mentioned.

cj415.text: He turns to take arrows on the other side; arrows even, boat level, he goes back.

cj416.text: The turn I asked you to remember: here, it's to keep the boat from capsizing.

cj417.text: But this passage is just 38 characters.

cj418.text: No fog, no straw, no numbers, and nobody says thanks.

cj419.text: In all of the Records, notes included, "take arrows" appears only here.

cj420.text: To take arrows is passive; the text never says he kept them.

cj422.text: No proof; we can only say the move is identical.

cj423.text: We think this looks more like a near-capsize mishap than a clever plan.

cj424.text: And in the same note, right beside it, Pei Songzhi copied another book.

cj501.text: It's the Wu Li, by Hu Chong of Wu;

cj502.text: that order we mentioned is here.

cj503.text: Sun Quan challenged again and again; Cao stayed put; so Sun Quan sailed up to Cao's camp himself.

cj504.text: Cao's generals took it as a challenge and wanted to charge; Cao said, Sun Quan wants to see my army.

cj505.text: He ordered his army in order: no shooting at will.

cj506.text: And Sun Quan wasn't in a big boat, but a light one.

cj507.text: Strangely, the boat turns here too: it goes five or six li, turns back, and plays music all the way.

cj508.text: Cao, at the fleet: A son should be like Sun Zhongmou.

cj509.text: Cao Cao was nearly sixty; Sun Quan, just over thirty.

cj510.text: Both books describe the same visit by Sun Quan.

cj511.text: The shooting in one becomes no shooting in the other.

cj512.text: And the two authors came from opposite sides of the war.

cj514.text: In Yuanjia 6, the year 429, he presented his notes to the emperor;

cj515.text: his memorial set the rule: when accounts differ and can't be judged, copy them all for reference.

cj516.text: So here he adds no comment.

cj517.text: And which side did later historians believe?

cj518.text: Sima Guang, writing the Zizhi Tongjian on Ruxu,

cj520.text: and Sun Quan's letter: "Spring floods are rising; you'd best leave fast."

cj521.text: But the Weilüe's arrow-laden boat: left out;

cj522.text: the Wu Li's light boat and order: left out too.

cj524.text: Read only the Zizhi Tongjian, and you'd never know of this boat.

cj525.text: Remember the opening question? In Jian'an 18, where was Zhuge Liang?

cj526.text: Guarding Jing Province with Guan Yu; that month, not at Ruxu.

cj527.text: Sun Quan asked Liu Bei for help; Liu Bei, in Yi Province, never came.

cj528.text: Per history, Zhou Yu's man Huang Gai lit the Red Cliffs fire;

cj529.text: Zhuge Liang was the alliance envoy.

cj530.text: The Records of the Three Kingdoms has no arrow borrowing.

cj532.text: He'd died of illness 3 years before.

cj533.text: So this file is closed: the earliest record we found of that turn

cj534.text: isn't on Zhuge Liang's boat, but Sun Quan's.

cj535.text: If you wrote it, who'd be at the prow?

cj536.text: We tell only what the records hold; subscribe to open files with us.
